decision: The demo proves three local-first loops: job discovery with distance, independently sourced profile/resume updates, and minimal daily/weekly work reports. Advanced matching and application tracking are deferred.
why: This preserves the full product intent while keeping the first implementation demonstrable.

decision: Store and use the exact home address only locally; use rotating nearby landmarks for external queries; obtain public job-location coordinates externally and compute final straight-line distance to the exact local coordinate on-device.
why: The user requires location-aware job discovery without disclosing the exact residence externally.

decision: Job discovery cannot directly modify the personal profile or resume; profile/resume updates use only user-imported or confirmed evidence, and work-report promotion requires confirmation.
why: The user explicitly requires resume updating and job discovery to remain isolated.

decision: Scheduled public-data reads and updates to pre-authorized local records are allowed; applications, messages, uploads, account authorization, and all other external writes require explicit user confirmation.
why: This is the agreed autonomy boundary for the demo.

decision: Root goal.md is the highest-priority product and boundary contract; goal/ contains subordinate architecture, research, plan, decisions, and append-only implementation records. Technical documents cannot silently change product intent.
why: The user requires a goal directory that remains aligned with the confirmed intent while becoming implementation-ready.

decision: Use the pinned and trimmed FastAPI full-stack template as the application base, LangGraph OSS as local orchestration, React/TypeScript for the dashboard, PostgreSQL for business data and checkpoints, APScheduler in a separate worker, and Docker Compose for local runtime.
why: This balances local-first constraints, implementation maturity, portfolio recognition, and a manageable demo scope.

decision: Remote GPT or other AI models are injected through a project-owned ModelProvider gateway. Local code performs parsing, minimization, policy checks, schema validation, and persistence; exact address, exact home coordinates, secrets, unrelated files, and the full database are blocked from outbound requests.
why: The user wants remote AI capability combined with a local agent without sacrificing the agreed privacy boundary.

decision: Clone the FastAPI template into a unique temporary directory, inspect its license and instructions, record a pinned commit, and selectively import declared application paths without copying upstream Git history or agent instructions. Use JobSpy, LangGraph, MarkItDown, and JSON Resume through pinned dependencies or schemas.
why: This preserves provenance and mature engineering structure while keeping MiniWorld's goal and Git history authoritative.

decision: Execute the implementation as a repository-wide bootstrap with explicit commit boundaries: goal baseline, pinned upstream import, local single-user reduction, feature loops, verification, and documentation. Do not push publicly or use real personal data/secrets while the user is away.
why: The user asked for autonomous progress, Git management, a runnable demo, tests, README updates, and accumulated decisions without intent drift.

decision: Run LangGraph OSS entirely in the local API/worker environment with PostgreSQL checkpoints; LangGraph Cloud and LangSmith are optional future services, not Demo dependencies.
why: The user explicitly confirmed the local LangGraph route and wants a technically current, job-market-recognizable project without weakening local-first constraints.

decision: Provide a network-free deterministic demo mode and a separately enabled live mode; persist and display the mode so test data or inference cannot be presented as live results.
why: The Demo must be reproducible without secrets while still supporting verifiable real-source and remote-model integration when the user configures them.

decision: Finish and validate the deterministic local runtime before live integrations, then complete the three business loops, dashboard, container validation, and documentation without using real personal data or secrets.
why: This is the safest reproducible route to the full requested Demo and preserves the explicit demo/live boundary.

decision: Keep real frontend/API operation, deterministic demo evidence, live public-read evidence, and privacy evidence distinct; fixed data or framework presence cannot substitute for live job-source validation.
why: This makes completion measurable and prevents technical implementation from overstating or changing the user's requested internet job-discovery capability.

decision: Prefer a company public ATS/Job Board GET API, beginning with a Lever Postings adapter, before best-effort JobSpy scraping. Keep every application POST endpoint outside current authorization.
why: The pinned JobSpy package exposes only LinkedIn, Indeed, and ZipRecruiter and the tested sources returned 403/451; Lever documents a public, stable-ID, read-only JSON path without changing the product goal.

decision: Label target architecture decomposition separately from the actual v0.5 graph nodes; only goal checklist evidence and implementation records establish completion.
why: The architecture document intentionally decomposes more nodes and recovery behaviors than the current code, and design presence must not be reported as implementation.
